The recovery in Chinese seaborne crude oil imports has stalled month-to-date (Aug 1-15 data), per @Vortexa. China imported an average of ~6.8m b/d in the first two weeks of the month, down from ~7.3m b/d in July.

El Niño and its impact on the global energy system

Sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean have climbed to a record high for the time of year, causing forecasters to predict a very strong El Niño will form in the final months of 2026.  

Surface temperatures averaged about 29.6°C last week, up from 26.6°C at the same time last year, according to data from the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. 

Temperatures were 1°C higher than the previous record for the time of year and 2.7°C above the long-term seasonal average, indicating exceptional warmth across the region. 

Sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific are a key driver of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) phenomenon, the single largest influence on weather patterns at seasonal scale worldwide. 

ENSO has significant impacts on the energy production and consumption – including hurricane formation in the Atlantic, winter temperatures and heating demand in the United States, and hydroelectric generation in South America ...

BRENT’s six-month calendar spread is trading in a backwardation of just under $10 per barrel implying traders see crude supplies relatively restricted in the short term. The spread has eased from a recent high of nearly $19 in late July but is still much tighter than the small contango reported at the start of last month before the ceasefire between the United States and Iran broke down. From an empirical perspective, the spread is consistent with some tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz but flows remaining far below normal and where they were when the ceasefire was in effect:

Here’s a brief recap of the oil math:

- Draws are currently concentrated in oil-on-water and China onshore crude inventories.

- Global product inventories remain low and are drawing counterseasonally.

- OECD crude inventories are seeing builds but will reverse to draws.

- Oman Lane is transiting ~5 million b/d of crude, or 2.5 VLCCs a day.

- The global oil deficit is clocked at ~3 million b/d, with visible oil inventories drawing ~1.5 million b/d.

Here’s NYT’s article: How the U.S. Navy Is Helping Get Oil Through the Strait of Hormuz

Only a few oil tankers braved Iran’s attacks to go through the Strait of Hormuz for much of the war, leading to a drastic reduction in how much crude reached world markets.

But since May, the U.S. military has played a crucial role in getting millions of barrels of oil through the strait, helping to keep oil prices from rising further.

The operation stealthily shepherds tankers through the southern part of the strait on routes close to Oman. Iran effectively controls which ships go through its side of the strait, opposite Oman.
Before the war, about 15 million barrels of crude oil a day went through the Strait of Hormuz. In July, tankers using U.S. protected routes transported around five million barrels of oil daily out of the Persian Gulf, according to analysts.

The effort goes beyond escorting outbound tankers with oil on board. The U.S. military is helping empty tankers enter the Gulf from the Arabian Sea through the strait, pick up oil from UAE, Bahrain and Kuwait, and then exit.

"We have been controlling the southern lane of the Strait of Hormuz for two months now. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps can be a nuisance, but they don't control the strait. We do," one of the U.S. officials, who has direct knowledge of the matter, said.

US claim:

1. 15-20 ship transits via southern Omani route
2. 10 MMbpd of oil flow (and supporting inbound tankers)

That’s a lot of oil, and much more than we’re currently seeing. 

7-day avg confirmed transits peaked in first week of August at ~7.5 MMbpd, by our view.

August avg nearer 5 MMbpd, or half US claim.

We’re likely undercounting actual transits, but it feels like a stretch that they’re managing to get *double* that volume out entirely undetected—no sign of loadings, or where these ships may be landing on the other end.
